power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.221", Sentence = "Red dashed lines are OLS trends, with significant positive trends for the Rowland, Fisher, and Reeves datasets, (OLS slopes +0.0007 to +0.0037, all p < 0.001), while not significant on Geschwind (p = 0.221)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. info.title: Cross-Symptoms Interactions Fail to Predict Future Symptom States Across Four Ecological Momentary Assessment Datasets

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								Psychological Methods Lab
								Philipps-Universität Marburg
								
									Germany

text.text: Symptom networks have emerged as a popular framework for characterizing the interactions among psychiatric symptoms.
Estimated from longitudinal ecological momentary assessment (EMA) recordings, they promise individualized insights into psychopathology and its treatment.
Yet whether these networks can be robustly estimated from the short, noisy, and irregularly sampled time series typical of EMA studies remains an open question.
We address this through the lens of predictive validity: do estimated cross-symptom connections improve forecasts of future symptom states?
In a systematic analysis spanning four public EMA datasets covering different symptoms and sampling schemes, we find that they largely do not.

In 273 of 313 participants, symptom networks are outperformed by networks that only use every individual symptom's past to predict its future, indicating that estimated cross-symptom connections tend to worsen out-of-sample predictions rather than improve them.

This pattern holds across estimation strategies from unregularized Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to multilevel hierarchical modeling and nonlinear statespace models, suggesting that cross-symptom connections are difficult to identify given the characteristics of real EMA data.

Simulation studies support this interpretation, showing that even when ground-truth data is generated by a network model mirroring realistic EMA conditions, cross-symptom structure is often not recovered with sufficient precision to yield a predictive advantage.

These findings raise questions about the interpretive framework built on idiographic symptom networks, and suggest that progress may require either measurement designs that make cross-symptom influence more identifiable, or models with less ambitious inferential targets than the recovery of directed cross-symptom effects.

Emotional states and psychiatric symptoms emerge from an interplay of intrinsic processes, such as interactions among psychological states or symptoms that influence one another, and extrinsic influences via a constant stream of environmental events and social contexts.
The network perspective on psychopathology has gained prominence [1], conceptualizing mental disorders as networks of symptoms that causally influence one another.
text.formatted: The network perspective on psychopathology has gained prominence <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, conceptualizing mental disorders as networks of symptoms that causally influence one another.

text.text: In depression, for instance, insomnia causes exhaustion, exhaustion results in anhedonia, and anhedonia further lowers mood, which in turn disrupts sleep.
A network model fit to symptom data, so is the hope, can capture how these self-sustaining cycles emerge.
This framing leans heavily on the assumption that internal, symptom-to-symptom dynamics dominate the system's evolution.
If this is true, meaningful predictive structure should be extractable from symptom time series alone.
If external, unobserved factors dominate instead, the system may fundamentally resist such efforts, and symptom evolution will appear driven by noise [2].
text.formatted: If external, unobserved factors dominate instead, the system may fundamentally resist such efforts, and symptom evolution will appear driven by noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Yet internal dynamics are not directly observable, but we can only infer them from how symptoms covary over time.
This inferential problem has been approached in two ways.
Early network research relied predominantly on cross-sectional, between-person data, estimating average symptom-to-symptom relationships across a sample.
This approach faces well-documented limitations.

Estimated networks are often supported by too little evidence for individual edges to be interpreted with confidence [3], and typical study sample sizes yield poor sensitivity for recovering true edges [4].
text.formatted: Estimated networks are often supported by too little evidence for individual edges to be interpreted with confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, and typical study sample sizes yield poor sensitivity for recovering true edges <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: More fundamentally, interpretations of cross-sectional networks conflate between-person and within-person variation, while psychiatric symptoms exhibit substantial non-ergodicity: population-level averages may poorly predict individual trajectories [5; 6; 7].
text.formatted: More fundamentally, interpretations of cross-sectional networks conflate between-person and within-person variation, while psychiatric symptoms exhibit substantial non-ergodicity: population-level averages may poorly predict individual trajectories <ref type="bibr">[5; 6; 7]</ref>.

text.text: A network estimated across people, in other words, need not resemble the dynamics within each individual.
Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA, [8]) offers the promise of capturing symptom evolution in situ, sampling how symptoms unfold in everyday life.
text.formatted: Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>) offers the promise of capturing symptom evolution in situ, sampling how symptoms unfold in everyday life.

text.text: The widespread adoption of smartphones has made it feasible to collect dense temporal data per person [9; 10].
text.formatted: The widespread adoption of smartphones has made it feasible to collect dense temporal data per person <ref type="bibr">[9; 10]</ref>.

text.text: Modeled with Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models, EMA data permits estimation of how symptoms at one time point predict symptoms at the next within individuals.
These person-specific network models enable simple visualizations [11], and promise individualized insight into symptom dynamics and potential treatment targets [12].
text.formatted: These person-specific network models enable simple visualizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, and promise individualized insight into symptom dynamics and potential treatment targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Concretely, a VAR model predicts each symptom's rating at a given timestep from the rating of all symptoms at the preceding timestep.

Its diagonal coefficients capture how strongly a symptom persists from one measurement to the next, while its off-diagonal coefficients capture influence between symptoms and are what is drawn as the edge of a symptom network.
An Autoregressive model(AR) model is the same model with those off-diagonal terms fixed to zero, therefore each symptom is predicted from its own history alone.
Yet an important question remains largely unaddressed: do these person-specific network models actually "work"?

If the premise of the network approach that symptom-to-symptom influence exert substantial causal influence holds, then the cross-symptom links a network model recovers should carry predictive information about a symptom's future.

Virtually no study in the idiographic network literature has tested this directly, until recently, where Fechtelpeter et al. [13] found that network models performed significantly worse even than simple baselines, and Zhang et al. [14] show that the time series lengths used throughout the idiographic network literature fall well short of what is required for estimated networks to be adequately powered.
text.formatted: Virtually no study in the idiographic network literature has tested this directly, until recently, where Fechtelpeter et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> found that network models performed significantly worse even than simple baselines, and Zhang et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> show that the time series lengths used throughout the idiographic network literature fall well short of what is required for estimated networks to be adequately powered.

text.text: These results put into question whether cross-symptom network estimation yields any predictive advantage, motivating the investigation we present here.

We build on [13] methodology, using an expanding window train-test validation (see Fig. 1) across four publicly available EMA datasets [15; 12; 16; 17], covering a broad spectrum spanning symptom dimensionality, sampling frequency, study length, clinical population (anxiety, depression, PTSD, and affect regulation), and preprocessing strategies.

text.text: We further investigate different network estimation strategies, moving from simple unregularised networks, different regularisation strategies, to more complex hierarchical models and nonlinear state space models.

Across this range of datasets, model families, and design choices, we find that models based on crosssymptom structure consistently add no predictive value beyond a symptom's own history, and mostly fail to outperform naive persistence or median forecasts.

We argue that our results indicate that this problem might more generally not be solvable by better models, but an intrinsic property of EMA data at realistic noise levels and study lengths, where robust and persistent cross-symptom dynamics (if they exist) are not reliably discoverable in principle.

text.text: The central question for network psychopathology is whether estimated symptom-to-symptom connections carry genuine predictive information.

Fig. 2 answers this directly: across all four datasets, all VAR models produce higher forecast error than AR models in the overwhelming majority of participants (overall: 273/313, p < 10 -40 ; per-dataset: Fisher 40/40, p < 10 -12 ;Reeves 20/20, p < 10 -6 ;Rowland 124/125, p < 10 -35 ;Geschwind 89/128, p < 10 -5 ).

text.text: Since AR models are a restricted special case of VAR models in which all off-diagonal elements of the transition matrix are constrained to zero, the fact that this constrained model consistently outperforms the full VAR means that the estimated cross-symptom connections do not merely fail to help, but actively introduce noise that degrades prediction ("overfitting").
This result is consistent across clinical populations, sampling frequencies, and preprocessing strategies.
Crucially, we find that these results hold independent of the precise estimation strategy of the network model, but observe unregularized networks are consistently worse.
This holds even for hierarchical estimation, which could be considered a potential remedy for the problem of short individual-level time series.

For the Geschwind dataset, the original study already relied on such hierarchical estimation, using the multilevel VAR (mlVAR, see 4.2.2 for details) framework introduced in Bringmann et al. [15], which places a hierarchical prior over individual transition matrices and yields both a population-level estimate (B pop ) and individually adapted predictions (B s ).

At the one-day-ahead horizon, this baseline becomes easy to outperform as autocorrelation decays, but all models then either converge toward the global median predictor, or perform worse than it.

text.text: A natural objection to the results so far is that the expanding-window design is unfair to VAR: validation begins at short training windows where the additional cross-symptom parameters cannot yet be estimated, and the simpler AR model benefits.
Fig. 3 (top row) tests this by plotting the difference in mean absolute error (MAE) between AR and VAR against training window size.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">3</ref> (top row) tests this by plotting the difference in mean absolute error (MAE) between AR and VAR against training window size.

text.text: VAR performance does improve with more data on Rowland, Fisher, and Reeves, while the trend is not significant on Geschwind, where the training range spans only four days.
The gap nonetheless never closes, regardless of how much data the model has seen.

While this confirms the results from Fig. 2 hold even if maximum training data is provided, the narrowing gap raises the question whether additional training data allow LASSO-VAR to discover genuine cross-symptom dynamics (in which case the closing of the gap is encouraging, and we just need more data), or whether it primarily causes the model to discard off-diagonal terms, effectively driving VAR toward AR.

text.text: The steepness of the decline scales with the number of free cross-symptom parameters: Geschwind, with six symptoms, shows the smallest decline, while Fisher and Reeves, with 21 and 20 items respectively, show the steepest.

In these two datasets the decline tracks the narrowing MAE gap closely, and the two asymptotes (AR-VAR gap approaching zero in the top row, off-diagonal norm reaching zero in the bottom row) are reached at roughly similar training windows, indicating that VAR improves by becoming like an AR model.

text.text: To gain further insight into these two interpretations (genuine cross-symptom structure surviving regularization vs. convergence on AR), we carried out an additional diagnostic analysis.

The autocorrelation structure of symptoms can arise either from a symptom's own persistence (sadness now tends to mean sadness later) or from another symptom's influence (anger now keeps sadness elevated later).

When symptoms are strongly correlated with one another, as they typically are in EMA data, these two explanations correspond to highly collinear predictors, so a joint model can only apportion variance between them via structural assumptions such as regularization.

As an approximate way to probe this collinearity, we regressed each symptom's own AR(1) history out of its time series and recomputed cross-symptom correlations on the residuals, which indicates how much of the raw cross-symptom correlation could plausibly be attributed to shared autocorrelation rather than direct coupling.

Fig. 7 shows that temporal (lag-1) cross-correlations drop substantially after residualization across all four datasets (25-48% reduction), and in three of four, including Rowland, the remaining correlation is statistically indistinguishable from what uncoupled time series of the same length produce by chance.

Given the approximate nature of this diagnostic, however, we do not treat it as conclusive on its own.
We examine the conditions under which genuine cross-symptom terms could in principle be recovered more directly via simulation studies below (Sect.2.3).

The failure of linear VAR models might further be attributed to two simplifying assumptions: that symptom dynamics are linear, and that they operate in the directly observed symptom space rather than an unobserved latent space.

Both assumptions are routinely questioned in the psychiatric modelling literature, where concepts such as multistability, attractor dynamics, and nonlinear switching between mood states [19] are frequently invoked to motivate more expressive model classes.

text.text: We therefore ask whether moving beyond linear observation-space models recovers the predictive structure that VAR fails to capture.
To test this, we trained Almost-Linear Recurrent Neural Networks (AL-RNNs, [20; 21]).

text.text: AL-RNNs generalise linear dynamical systems by allowing a small number of units to implement nonlinear switching between linear subregions, while the remainder of the network remains linear.
While there are many candidate nonlinear model classes one might consider, we focus on AL-RNNs for two reasons.

First, the P = 0 case recovers a linear state-space model estimated via gradient descent, hence effectively a VAR with different implicit regularisation, providing a direct connection to the model class already examined.
Second, increasing P allows us to tune nonlinearity continuously, so the question of whether expressivity helps can be answered systematically.

We present an illustrative analysis on the Fisher dataset, since its regular sampling structure directly satisfies the temporal assumptions of sequential recurrent models, but found consistent results with the other datasets as well.
We trained AL-RNN on the EMA data, varying the number of piecewise-linear nonlinear units P ∈ {0, 5, 10}.

Unlike VAR models, which are fit in a single step, models of this class are fit iteratively, where parameters are adjusted in small increments, with each pass through the data (a training epoch) reducing the error on the training set.

Plotting out-of-sample error against training time thus provides a natural diagnostic for the point at which a model has captured the reproducible structure in the data from the point at which it begins fitting noise, with error on held-out data first falling and then rising again.

Crucially, no model at any level of nonlinearity outperforms the AR baseline at any point during optimisation.
While more nonlinear models overfit more slowly, their pattern is very similar to that of the linear AL-RNN.
Hence whatever an optimally early-stopped model would recover here, does not provide predictive value beyond the symptom's own history.

Therefore, cross-symptom structure these models learn is, by this measure, sample-specific noise, analogously to the linear case.

While we again cannot exclude that nonlinear models could in principle capture more complex cross-symptom dynamics, without sufficiently strong priors these models face even greater identifiability pressure than VAR models.

Finally, the convergence of all estimation strategies toward the same predictive ceiling suggests that the failure of network models is not a consequence of how coefficients are estimated, but of what kind of data they are estimated from.
To interpret this, we turn to simulations in which the ground-truth network is known, and ask what a given AR-versus-VAR forecast gap implies about how well that network has been recovered.
This step is necessary because in real EMA data the ground-truth connectivity is unknown and comparing forecasts is the only available test.

To this end we conducted simulations using ground-truth VAR models with autoregressive coefficients drawn to produce lag-1 autocorrelation in the range observed in the empirical data (mean ≈ 0.5), while systematically varying network strength (magnitude of cross-lagged coefficients) and network density (the ratio of real edges vs. number of possible edges in A).

This paper set out to test whether idiographic VAR-based temporal network models estimated from EMA data demonstrate predictive validity.

Across four independent datasets spanning 313 participants and diverse clinical populations and symptom batteries, the answer is consistently negative, where VAR-based symptom network models are outperformed by their own restricted autoregressive special case, i.e.
AR models, in the overwhelming majority of participants.
This means the estimated cross-symptom connections do not only fail to add predictive value, but actively degrade forecasting accuracy, a signature of overfitting.

This finding holds across all tested estimation strategies, from unregularised OLS, LASSO regularisation, stepwise SEM selection, hierarchical estimation, and nonlinear extensions, which all converge to the same predictive ceiling.
The invariance of this ceiling implies that the problem lies in what can be identified from the data rather than in any particular estimation strategy.

Our simulation confirms that the empirically observed AR-versus-VAR forecast ratios (≈ 0.88-0.95) correspond to poor network recovery on all three metrics tested, even with a known ground-truth VAR process matched to the empirical autocorrelation.

Recovery does improve with denser, stronger networks and longer series, but it shows that the forecasting gaps we observe in practice are consistent with a true network existing yet being unrecoverable at realistic EMA time series lengths and coupling strengths.
Network inference from time series data is a recurring problem across fields, including synaptic connectivity estimated from spike trains [24], and gene regulatory networks [25].

text.text: A direct parallel can also be found in functional neuroimaging, where fMRI measures blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal as an indirect proxy for neural activity in each of a set of brain regions, sampled repeatedly over time.
The inferential task of estimating directed influence among brain regions is closely related, with the added complication that true couplings operate on a timescale faster than the sampling interval.

There, lag-based methods, including VAR-based network models [26], and more expressive approaches such as Dynamic Causal Modelling [27], have been reported to face identifiability problems of their own [28; 29] and to recover directionality only poorly from realistic BOLD data [30; 31], despite regular sampling, negligible missingness, absence of external factors, and longer recordings offering more favorable conditions than those found in EMA data.

text.text: Beyond the question of identifiability, our results are also suggestive about what kind of process could be underpinning the data.

Predictions are bracketed by the persistence baseline (predicting the next rating by the previous one) at the one-step horizon and the global median at the one-day horizon, which bears on the opening question of whether intrinsic symptom-to-symptom dynamics or extrinsic and unobserved influences dominate the system's evolution.
For a process with the martingale property, the current value is the optimal one-step predictor that no function of the observed history improves upon [32].
text.formatted: For a process with the martingale property, the current value is the optimal one-step predictor that no function of the observed history improves upon <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: That symptom trajectories are predicted near-optimally by their own last observed value bounds how much of their short-term evolution can be carried by deterministic within-system coupling at the timescale and resolution captured here.

Since EMA data only offers a partial window onto the underlying process, this is also consistent with symptom dynamics being driven by variation these measurements do not resolve, whether environmental events and social contexts absent from the symptom data, or symptom-to-symptom influence operating faster than the sampling interval.
We think these findings have implications beyond the specific models tested here.

Much of the network perspective's interpretive weight rests on individual edges: properties such as centrality indices and proposed intervention targets rely on directed coefficients of an estimated transition matrix.

We want to emphasize that recovering such coefficients is a considerably harder statistical problem than may be intuitively apparent, and has accordingly surfaced, as outlined before, in other fields where a similar problem has been pursued (e.g. [26]).

text.text: The conditions under which recovery succeeds (i.e. strong coupling combined with long recordings and low noise) may often not be met by the EMA protocols on which symptom network studies are typically based.

Claims about which symptom drives which can therefore rest on parameters that the data frequently cannot constrain, a pattern that persisted across every symptom set and every estimation strategy we tested.

Our results do not exclude that a protocol with a different symptom set, substantially fewer variables, denser sampling, or a population with stronger cross-symptom coupling could yield identifiable cross-symptom interactions.
What they do suggest is that this problem may be harder than its routine application assumes, which makes it less surprising that no estimator we tried recovered structure that improved prediction.

A reasonable prior going forward is that cross-symptom dynamics may not be reliably recoverable from EMA data unless the population, protocol, and dimensionality of the modeled system are chosen with this goal in mind.
We see several ways forward.

On the measurement side, new protocols can resolve unobserved factors that currently appear as noise, or increase identifiability by extending recordings and reducing the dimensionality of the modeled system.

The limitations of unimodal self-report have contributed to a shift toward multimodal designs incorporating physiological, behavioural, and environmental data [33], alongside explicit efforts to measure the external events and contextual shifts (e.g. social encounters, weather reports etc.) that pure symptom time series models have to absorb into the residual [34].

EMA data remain informative for many purposes [39]: mean symptom levels, intraindividual variance, and treatment-related trajectories are legitimate targets of analysis that fall outside the scope of our critique.

text.text: Our critique specifically concerns the interpretation of individual cross-lagged coefficients, and their failure to contribute meaningfully to out-of-sample forecasts.

We therefore propose out-of-sample comparison against the restricted autoregressive model as a routine validation step for idiographic network analyses, applicable to symptom sets, populations, protocols, and estimators beyond those examined here.
The test is inexpensive, requires no additional data collection, and provides a simple interpretable verification of the validity of cross-symptom coefficients.

When assessing that a network model is a good explanation of the data, we must distinguish between two problems: (1) a hidden network exists but is difficult to infer (a problem of identifiability), versus (2) the network framework itself poorly explains what drives the data (a problem of model misspecification).

This difference maps onto a broader methodological divide between statistical inference and machine learning approaches to model validation [40], which have been called the "two cultures" of statistical learning [41].

Machine learning, on the other hand, prioritizes out-of sample prediction without necessarily formalizing an explicit model of underlying mechanisms [42].

Forecast accuracy was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE): where errors are expressed in standardized units to enable aggregation across variables with different scales.
